doc.title: Harold Mabern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010

title: Being a blues pianist who understands jazz
summary: He says all jazz comes from the blues, recalls Jimmy Witherspoon and Joe Williams at the Half Note, lists musicians who came up through blues bands, and says Chicago required blues and singer accompaniment.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: Did you guys kind of have a separate half from the rock & roll and the pop music that was played on AM radio at the time? In other words, did you listen to the music that was getting all the airplay, the Chuck Berry and those guys? Did it affect you at all? © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

If it was good music yeah. And to this day I still do that because see I always tell people — somebody asked me a question and I said well you know I consider myself a blues piano player that understands the philosophy of jazz. So I told Fred and he said, “You said that?” He said, “I like that.” That’s what I am. I’m going to always be, because blues or jazz comes from the blues. Because here again, like I said, not to be redundant, there are a lot of jazz musicians who can swing, who can play jazz, but they can’t play the blues. You can’t teach that. It’s by nature or just being, or whatever. So that’s the way I feel. I mean if I had a choice to play “Rakin’ and Scrapin’” or one of my compositions or if somebody asks me, I’m going to take the blues because with me, the blues, I am the blues. Somebody else might say it, but I am the blues. That’s me. And don’t forget, I was working at the Half Note with Joe Williams, rest his soul, and Jimmy Witherspoon came down to see us. And Fred said — we were having a great time playing — so Spoon said, “Hey Joe, let me hear some blues.” So Joe Williams said, “Spoon, it’s too early for the blues.” Spoon said, “Joe it ain’t never too early for the blues.” It’s right. If you play with Milt Jackson you’d better know how to play the blues. That’s what I said. Charles Mingus said, “I wish I could write like Duke Ellington and play the blues.” So, so no, so I’ve always been attracted to the blues, even to this day, or anything that’s bluesy. You know, like Ahmad Jamal played with George Hudson’s Blues Band. That why if you listen to a lot of Ahmad’s compositions they’ve got the bluesy feeling to it. Clifford Brown played with Chris Powell and the Blue Flames blues band, or Bill Hardman, played Tiny Bradshaw, Jimmy — you know, so most of those — Stanley Turrentine, Coltrane, played with — Earl Bostic Rhythm & Blues band. Now you’ve got Louis Jordan and the Tympany Five. George Coleman and Jimmy Anastos played with B.B. King’s blues band, rhythm and blues. George Coleman took the first alto solo on “Woke Up This Morning” (my baby’s gone), that was a hit, you see, so we all came up through the blues. No when I listen to the radio now, or whatever, anything that’s bluesy or [inaudible] you know. I don’t listen to everything because most of the stuff is not worth it because the minute you hear it you say well that’s not my cup of tea. You can tell that it’s nothing happening, you know. But like I was going to Denver one time. And I’m on American Airlines and I’m going to Denver for eight weeks by myself. Cold. I’m going to be like the house band. And you know how you listen to the headphones on the airplane and I hear [scats] I said what is that, it’s so beautiful. Then it turned out to be Bobby Caldwell “What You Won’t Do for Love” which to this day is a big hit all over Japan. So I’m always attracted to anything that’s bluesy. Earth, Wind & Fire, Chaka Khan, whoever it is. If it’s bluesy. I didn’t listen like to like to Chuck Berry intentionally, but blues — Mulgrew Miller and I were talking about Little Milton Campbell and we were talking about B.B. B.B.’s great but Little Milton Campbell had some stuff together © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

and he was from Greenwood, Mississippi where Mulgrew Miller is from. Little Milton Campbell. He could sing “If Walls Could Talk” and “Poor Man Blues” you see. And see in Chicago you had to play the blues, not in New York City. You go on the south side of Chicago or the west side, and you had to know how to play some blues. And you had to know how to play for singers. And see those are the two foundations. So when I got to Chicago it was no big deal ‘cause I already knew kind of how to play the blues from being in Memphis, Tennessee. Now what I get with the singers, now that becomes my accompanying skills. And those are the two things I think that have helped me as much as it can help me, is being able to play the blues, being able to swing, knowing chord changes, know how to transpose, and know how to play for singers.
